selected.description: Profiles in History: Historical Auction 52 November 15, 2012 Highlights of the auction include: Thomas Jefferson (March 1, 1792) – Announcement of the Bill of Rights: Written as Secretary of State to the Governor of New Hampshire, this is the monumental, official circular letter announcing that three-fourths of the states had ratified the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution. Thomas Jefferson (1806) – Address to the Cherokee Nation: A museum-grade, fully handwritten presidential manuscript containing the actual diplomatic address Jefferson delivered to the Chiefs of the Cherokee Nation regarding tribal sovereignty and early federal co-existence. John Tyler (1841) – The Succession Precedent Executive Order: Written on black-bordered mourning stationery immediately following the death of William Henry Harrison, this urgent cabinet assembly order marks the precise hour Tyler claimed the full title of President, permanently shattering the cabinet's claim that he was merely "Acting President". Abraham Lincoln (July 8, 1863) – The Post-Gettysburg Civil War Draft Quota: Signed a mere five days after the bloody conclusion of the Battle of Gettysburg, this formal executive command orders a strict military draft of troops from Connecticut to reinforce shattered Union forces.Benjamin Franklin (March 13, 1775) – The Pre-Revolutionary Departure Letter: Written from London just eight days before Franklin fled back to America and three weeks before the Battle of Lexington, marking the exact moment he abandoned peaceful reconciliation with Great Britain. George Washington (February 14, 1779) – British Supply Passport: Bearing Washington’s complete, intact red wax coat-of-arms seal from his winter camp at Middlebrook, this document authorized a British vessel to supply 5,000 captive British and Hessian troops (the "Convention Army" captured at Saratoga). George Washington (February 2, 1777) – The "Fireside Duty" Warning: Written from Morristown to Rhode Island's governor, Washington fiercely condemns the state for offering separate bounty pay and promises of local, safe duty, warning that subverting the Continental Army is an "indirect breach of the Union". Ulysses S. Grant (November 6, 1861) – The Battle Order that Launched His Career: Written at Cairo, Illinois, this critical tactical order outlines the military ruse that successfully deceived the Confederates and won the Battle of Belmont, catapulting Grant to national fame and Abraham Lincoln's personal attention. Yuri Gagarin (January 24, 1968) – Moon Program Aerodynamic Manuscript: A highly technical, hand-corrected research paper detailing wind-tunnel analysis and computer calculations aimed at landing the Soviets on the moon. Tragically, his illustrations analyzing aircraft flight angles were drawn just two months before he died in a flight-training crash. Winston Churchill (June 1943) – Post-War Imperial Civil Aviation Draft: A highly strategic draft page completely reworked in Churchill's red ink, outlining his plan to entangle American corporate interests in a loosely regulated universal aviation framework to transform rising U.S. air power into a bulwark for the post-war British Empire. Alexander Graham Bell (April 17, 1917) – The Houseboat Emergency Letter: A 4-page letter written to his wife detailing a treacherous, frozen wilderness voyage through Nova Scotia. This is the only known letter in private hands where the legendary inventor explicitly details using his own creation—the telephone—to coordinate a survival rescue. Vincent van Gogh (1890) – The Final Year Letter: A heart-wrenching letter written in French during the final months of his life, featuring the devastating philosophical observation that "illnesses are there to make us remember again that we are not made of wood".Martin Luther King Jr. (November 22, 1965) – Citizenship Education Letter: Written on Southern Christian Leadership Conference letterhead, King meticulously details his "CEP" literacy program, designed to teach underprivileged, newly enfranchised Black citizens how to read so they could safely protect and utilize their newly won ballot. Other items included in the auction: John Adams Document (January 4, 1797): Signed as Vice President, officially accepting Kentucky's electoral votes from the historic and acrimonious 1796 election that made him the second U.S. President. John Adams Letter (May 19, 1798): Written during the height of the Quasi-War crisis with France, thanking citizens of Hamilton, Massachusetts, for pledging their lives and property to defend American liberty. John Quincy Adams Letter (May 25, 1820): Written while serving as Secretary of State, insisting on paying for a gift of wine to rigidly uphold the constitutional principle against public servants accepting foreign presents. Millard Fillmore Document (July 14, 1851): Presidential appointment (co-signed by Daniel Webster) naming an Austrian Consul for the booming, Gold Rush-era port of San Francisco. Benjamin Franklin Letter (March 13, 1775): Written from London just eight days before Franklin fled to America and three weeks before the Battle of Lexington, marking the final collapse of his efforts to negotiate peace with Britain. Abraham Lincoln Draft Order (July 8, 1863): Formal executive command ordering a military draft of forces from Connecticut to reinforce Union troops during the height of the American Civil War. Ulysses S. Grant Pamphlet (1865): Inscribed copy of Grant's official military report detailing the final year of the Civil War, explicitly highlighting his direct surrender communications with Robert E. Lee at Appomattox. Jefferson Davis Letter (January 22, 1874): Written by the former Confederate President, privately addressing congressional moves to exclude him from political amnesty. Jefferson Davis Letter (January 22, 1876): Davis requests to be formally removed from an amnesty bill so his compatriots can be pardoned, while remaining proudly unrepentant of his secessionist political stance. Chester A. Arthur Letter (November 13, 1886): The former President requests that legendary sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens create his official marble bust for the U.S. Senate Chamber.Progressive & Gilded Age Figures Andrew Carnegie Inscription (November 9, 1874): Signed quotation outlining his iconic philosophy on philanthropy, declaring surplus wealth a sacred trust to be used for the public good during one's lifetime. Susan B. Anthony Letter (January 10, 1900): Written on National-American Woman Suffrage Association letterhead, championing women's right to petition Congress as their only political voice while remaining disenfranchised. James Buchanan Letter (March 28, 1853): Written prior to his presidency, illustrating the intense burdens of political patronage as he laments being bombarded by endless state employment requests. Winston Churchill Statement (February 16, 1920): Written from the War Office during the rise of Soviet Bolshevism, asserting that U.S. and British unity is the only true guarantee for future world peace. Winston Churchill Letter (May 27, 1942): A rare wartime prime ministerial letter intervening in a special election, urging voters to maintain resolve to "cleanse the world from Hitlerism".Winston Churchill Letter (April 17, 1943): Prime ministerial letter sharply criticizing a satirical cartoon in Punch magazine to defend the dignity of General Montgomery and his North African Eighth Army. Winston Churchill Customs Document (December 27, 1945): Form filled out prior to his pivotal 1946 journey to America, where he ultimately delivered his iconic post-war "Iron Curtain" speech. Winston Churchill Signed Portrait (Undated): A signed portrait capturing a youthful Churchill at his writing desk, symbolizing his journey toward becoming a global statesman. Chiang Kai-Shek Letter (June 30, 1944): Written from Chungking to U.S. General Hap Arnold, praising the success of the first B-29 bombing missions against mainland Japan, made possible by massive manual Chinese labor. Dwight D. Eisenhower Letter (May 12, 1943): Written from Algiers immediately following the Axis surrender in Tunisia, reflecting immense relief at the conclusion of the pivotal North African Campaign. Dwight D. Eisenhower Letter (October 19, 1944): Written from Belgium, emphasizing that military personnel must avoid partisan political campaigns and remain loyal to the sitting President. Dwight D. Eisenhower Letter (January 15, 1945): Deeply personal letter to his wife Mamie penned just days before the end of the Battle of the Bulge, detailing the staggering mental toll and human destruction of the war. Dwight D. Eisenhower Portrait (Undated): Inscribed to Hollywood star and political figure George Murphy, who served as a prominent mentor within California's Republican party. Albert Einstein Letter (June 20, 1950): Written ten months after the first Soviet atomic test, stressing that a minimal World Government framework is desperately needed to avoid total nuclear annihilation. Calvin Coolidge Inscribed Photograph (December 1919): Inscribed with his core political philosophy, asserting that public office is a duty of cooperation rather than a game for "public plunder". Calvin Coolidge Letter (May 29, 1926): A presidential letter to a Rhode Island campaign supporter reflecting on his successful 1924 election run. Calvin Coolidge Letter (February 7, 1929): Written weeks before leaving office, offering a personal, delayed thank-you note for a Christmas watch and chain. Gerald R. Ford Inscribed Book (October 1, 1980): Inscription inside his book Portrait of the Assassin, where the former President fiercely defends the original, contested findings of the Warren Commission regarding JFK's assassination. Jimmy Carter Letter (November 26, 1973): Written as Governor of Georgia, sharing an intimate reflection on his childhood experiencing Christmas on a rural farm without electricity or running water. Jean Paul Getty Check (January 2, 1982/1942): A signed personal financial artifact from the historic American oil billionaire. John Hancock Commission (December 10, 1776): Signed just two weeks before Washington crossed the Delaware; commissions a second lieutenant into the Continental military during a dire phase of the revolution. William Howe Financial Order (May 27, 1777): Signed by the British Commander-in-Chief in New York; directs major war funding to bolster British fortifications and barracks in Nova Scotia. John Paul Jones Letter (August 17, 1785): Naval hero writes directly to Thomas Jefferson in Paris; demands federal intervention to secure withheld Revolutionary War prize money for his Alliance privateer crew. Thomas Jefferson Shipping List (August 31, 1790): Personal manuscript inventory detailing household furniture packed for Monticello; documents the transition of the federal government from New York to Philadelphia and notes items owned by traveling companion James Madison. Thomas Jefferson Letter (March 1, 1792): Sent as Secretary of State to the Governor of New Hampshire; serves as the monumental official announcement of the final ratification of the American Bill of Rights. John Hancock Document (November 17, 1792): Executed as Governor of Massachusetts; formally appoints Revolutionary War militia veteran Azor Orne as an early U.S. presidential elector. John Langdon Letter (June 30, 1792): Written by the Constitutional Convention delegate and first Senate president pro-tempore regarding a commercial shipping invoice from France. Thomas Jefferson Land Grant (February 16, 1802): Presidential vellum document co-signed by James Madison; allocates 327 acres of frontier land to refugees fleeing British-controlled Canada. Thomas Jefferson Letter (July 2, 1820): Late-life correspondence praising a translated history of the American Revolution; passionately reaffirms his lifelong "holy enthusiasm for liberty and independence". Andrew Jackson Advice Document (June 9, 1833): President Jackson pens moral encouragement onto a printed souvenir copy of Thomas Jefferson’s famous 1824 letter of advice to a young namesake. Ulysses S. Grant Quartermaster Record (February 1, 1853): Early peacetime document signed as a 30-year-old Brevet Captain in the Oregon Territory; highlights his early quartermaster duties and the personal financial hardships of frontier army life. Ulysses S. Grant Battle Order (November 6, 1861): Critical tactical order written at Cairo, Illinois; outlines a strategic ruse that won the Battle of Belmont and launched Grant into national fame. Abraham Lincoln Staff Endorsement (February 11, 1862): Presidential wartime endorsement approving William D. Whipple for a staff position under General John E. Wool. Andrew Johnson Military Letter (November 8, 1862): Sent as Military Governor of Tennessee to President Lincoln; desperately pleads for federal troop retention to protect vulnerable, pro-Union East Tennessee families from Confederate forces. Abraham Lincoln Draft Order (July 8, 1863): Framed draft directive signed just five days after the bloody conclusion of Gettysburg; orders a quota of 2,021 men from Connecticut amid mounting national conscription tensions. Andrew Johnson Pardon (October 25, 1866): Official executive warrant authorizing the presidential pardon of George Trenholm, the final Secretary of the Treasury for the Confederate States. Rutherford B. Hayes Letter (August 14, 1885): Written less than a week after attending Ulysses S. Grant's massive seven-mile funeral procession; muses that the immense public turnout proved the powerlessness of political calumny against Grant's legacy. Benjamin Harrison Letter (October 1, 1891): Presidential letter to a judge explaining the difficult administrative burdens and limitations of federal political patronage. Herbert Hoover Neutrality Letter (March 7, 1920): Written prior to his entry into the cabinet, meticulously refusing to authorize his name for the 1920 presidential nomination. Warren G. Harding White House Letters (January 1922): Presidential employment correspondence paired with First Lady Florence Harding's 1921 personal notes to family relatives. Herbert Hoover Dog Portrait (Undated): Signed campaign photograph featuring his pet German Shepherd "King Tut," an image widely distributed to soften Hoover's public persona for the 1928 election. John F. Kennedy Harvard Essay (March 21, 1957): Handwritten manuscript drafted on the back of an Alabama speech; reflects on the true essence of Harvard University and praises political mentor Professor Arthur Holcombe. John F. Kennedy Warm Springs Speech (October 10, 1960): Heavily annotated personal reading copy of a campaign speech delivered at FDR's Georgia home; forcefully outlines a vision for minority social reform to "open new doors to the negro". John F. Kennedy Dallas Speech (September 13, 1960): Original Cold War campaign transcript detailing a strong American posture to counter Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev; delivered along the exact motorcade route where he would be assassinated three years later. Lyndon B. Johnson Presentation Book (Christmas 1962): Biography inscribed as Vice President to President John F. Kennedy; features a poignant and unintendedly tragic wish for "peace and repose in 1963 and onward". John & Jacqueline Kennedy Guide Book (Christmas 1962): Inscribed leather copy of the first historic White House guidebook gifted to military aide Godfrey McHugh; McHugh would later guard JFK's casket on Air Force One following the Dallas tragedy. Martin Luther King Jr. Letter (November 22, 1965): Written on Southern Christian Leadership Conference letterhead to a school teacher; underscores the vital mission of his "Citizenship Education" program to teach basic literacy to disenfranchised southern Black citizens gaining the ballot. Lyndon B. Johnson Family Letter (July 14, 1970): Post-presidential letter to his young grandson contrasting early 20th-century automobiles with modern Apollo moon landings. Abraham Lincoln Allegiance Card (April 10, 1865): Executed just one day after General Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House; formally orders the release of a former Confederate soldier upon taking the prescribed oath of allegiance. Capt. Ira Goodnow Autograph Album (March 4, 1863): A comprehensive Civil War-era registry compiled by the House of Representatives Doorkeeper. Features more than 200 signatures, including President Lincoln, Vice President Hamlin, key cabinet officers (Seward, Stanton, Chase, Welles, Usher), and battlefield commanders like Grant and Sherman. Abraham Lincoln Prisoner Discharge (October 21, 1863): A presidential manuscript responding to a grieving widow's request. Lincoln coordinates with an Illinois representative to verify her story before officially discharging her surviving 18-year-old son, who had survived the Battle of Gettysburg in frail health after his older brother was mortally wounded there. Abraham Lincoln Presentation Book (1860): A first edition, first issue copy of the Political Debates between Hon. Abraham Lincoln and Hon. Stephen A. Douglas. Personally inscribed in pencil to his close political ally Jesse K. Dubois, who helped engineer Lincoln's 1860 presidential nomination. Dolley Madison Third-Person Letter (July 14, 1838): Written by the iconic former First Lady to former President John Quincy Adams, requesting the return of personal manuscripts he had been reviewing for her. James Madison Membership Certificate (January 1, 1834): Signed by the former President while serving as head of the American Colonization Society. Documents the historical movement to repatriate free African Americans to West Africa, which resulted in the founding of Liberia. James McHenry Revolutionary War Letter (July 26, 1781): Despatched from headquarters near Williamsburg to Major General Nathanael Greene. McHenry expresses anxiety over Lord Cornwallis' tactical maneuvers at Yorktown just weeks before the decisive Franco-American siege ended the war. William McKinley Signed Photograph (August 12, 1898): Oversized historical portrait captured by pioneering female photojournalist Frances Benjamin Johnston. Signed by President McKinley and key international diplomats inside the White House Cabinet Room immediately following the signing of the Peace Protocol that ended the Spanish-American War. William McKinley Executive Order (February 6, 1899): Official presidential warrant authorizing the U.S. seal to be affixed to the definitive Treaty of Paris, formally concluding the Spanish-American War and establishing the United States as a global colonial power. Charles Lindbergh Air Corps Letter (December 20, 1941): Penned a mere two weeks after the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. The famous aviator directly offers his services to General "Hap" Arnold, attempting to pivot away from his highly controversial, pre-war isolationist stance with the America First Committee. Richard Nixon Watergate Legal Document (August 29, 1973): Unsigned 6-page legal brief submitted by top White House defender Fred Buzhardt. Formally refutes a subpoena issued by the Senate Select Committee by asserting a sweeping claim of executive privilege over the White House taping system. Franklin D. Roosevelt Power of Attorney (March 22, 1932): Legal document appointing his son, James Roosevelt, as his lawful attorney to manage political delegates ahead of the 1932 Democratic National Convention. Franklin D. Roosevelt Letter on John Paul Jones (February 14, 1934): A presidential letter thanking an artist for a historical silhouette of Revolutionary War naval hero John Paul Jones. Franklin D. Roosevelt Signed Engraving (January 20, 1937): A presentation print depicting his second inaugural reviewing stand (modeled after Andrew Jackson's home, The Hermitage), affectionately inscribed to close New Deal architect Harry Hopkins. Franklin D. Roosevelt Signed Cabinet Photograph (Undated): Official Harris & Ewing group portrait signed by the President and his entire core cabinet, including historic figures like Frances Perkins and Henry Wallace. Franklin D. Roosevelt Pre-War Prediction Letter (March 25, 1939): A remarkably candid personal letter to Gertrude Ely written amidst the rapid collapse of European stability. FDR utilizes a vivid horse-racing metaphor to accurately predict a catastrophic global conflict that would burn down the "grandstand" of civilization. Franklin D. Roosevelt Vatican Envoy Letters (March 14, 1940): A pair of personal letters defending his appointment of steel industrialist Myron Taylor as a special peace envoy to Pope Pius XII. FDR strongly counters domestic Protestant criticisms regarding the separation of church and state. Franklin D. Roosevelt Election Campaign Letter (September 24, 1928): Written to his law partner Basil O’Connor while campaigning for Al Smith. Quotes a local Georgia carpenter to estimate local electoral opposition to Smith's historic, yet highly controversial, Catholic candidacy.Franklin D. Roosevelt Wartime Media Letter (May 6, 1942): A sharp presidential letter to Senator Lister Hill dismissing a controversial Saturday Evening Post column by Felix Morley, accusing the author of writing theoretical nonsense that "rejoices the heart of Hitler". Franklin D. Roosevelt Oglethorpe Inscription (1923): Inscribed inside a compilation book of Woodrow Wilson's achievements, noting that "Right will succeed in the end". Franklin D. Roosevelt Signed D-Day Prayer Book (Christmastide 1944): Copy number 45 of a limited 100-copy run printed by the Government Printing Office. Inscribed to his son John and daughter-in-law Anne, containing the full text of the national prayer he composed on the eve of the Normandy invasion. Theodore Roosevelt Centennial Speech (February 12, 1909): Large-format commemorative document signed by President Roosevelt at the cornerstone dedication of the Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site on the 100th anniversary of Lincoln's birth. Theodore Roosevelt WWI Frustration Letter (April 24, 1918): Written from Sagamore Hill to a family friend while all of Roosevelt's sons were deployed in Europe. Teddy vents extreme indignation at the Woodrow Wilson administration's slowness and military mismanagement, noting that a year into the war, American forces remain under-equipped. Theodore Roosevelt Pre-War Neutrality Protest (September 1, 1915): A private letter written shortly after the sinking of the Lusitania, fiercely criticizing President Wilson's neutrality policy and calling for a leader like Andrew Jackson to issue a "bugle call from the White House" to rouse the American public. Theodore Roosevelt Signed Rough Rider Photograph (December 10, 1905): A presidential presentation photograph inscribed to a former military comrade. Shows Roosevelt in his 1898 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry uniform, commemorating his famous charge up the San Juan Heights during his self-described "crowded hour". George Washington Family Cobbler Order (June 20, 1768): Written from Mount Vernon to a London craftsman; orders custom summer boots and leather shoes for himself, Master Custis, Miss Custis, and his servants. Notably includes specific feedback from Martha Washington, who was unsatisfied with a previous pair because they were "made out of bad material." George Washington Militia Letter (September 6, 1776): Dispatched from Continental Headquarters in New York to the President of the New York Committee of Safety; officially accepts the regional committee's strategic assessment against depleting farming communities by calling up additional local militia. George Washington British Supply Passport (February 14, 1779): Executed during the grueling winter encampment at Middlebrook, New Jersey, and bearing Washington’s complete red wax family coat-of-arms seal; authorizes a British supply ship, the Brig Lady Howe, to transport critical clothing and provisions through the lines to sustain 5,000 captive British and Hessian troops (the "Convention Army" captured at Saratoga) being held near Charlottesville, Virginia. George Washington Morristown Resignation Appeal (May 27, 1780): Written to Colonel Clement Biddle from headquarters at Morristown; passionately urges the colonel to withdraw his military resignation. Washington utilizes uncharacteristically urgent language, emphasizing that an "interesting juncture" is at hand as they imminently expect a French fleet and land army to arrive to fight the common enemy. George Washington Financial Warning (February 2, 1777): Dispatched from Morristown to Rhode Island Governor Nicholas Cooke shortly after the historic victories at Trenton and Princeton; severely admonishes the state for trying to attract recruits with uncoordinated colonial bonus pay and promises of easy "fireside" home service. Washington warns that this practice creates separate local interests that poison the collective Continental Army. George Washington Post-Presidency Reply (October 12, 1796): Written while serving his final months as the nation's first President, responding to affectionate praise from Virginia citizens regarding his iconic Farewell Address; eloquently expresses supreme confidence that the "good sense of my Countrymen" will always successfully guide them to choose an able Chief Executive without his presence. Woodrow Wilson Inscribed Portrait (Undated): A signed mezzotint engraving featuring a head-and-shoulders portrait of the 28th President. Woodrow Wilson Joint Session War Portrait (April 2, 1917): A highly historic photograph depicting the exact moment President Wilson delivered his War Message against Imperial Germany to a Joint Session of Congress, formally ending American isolationism; co-signed on the matting by Wilson, House Speaker Champ Clark, and Vice President Thomas Marshall. Woodrow Wilson Signed Cabinet Photograph (March 1913): Large boardroom group portrait signed by President Wilson and his entire original cabinet, including historic Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan and Treasury Secretary William G. McAdoo. Woodrow Wilson Paris Peace Letter (April 16, 1919): Written from Paris to the U.S. Minister to Belgium during the post-war negotiations; intimately reflects on a touching public parade where Belgian working-class citizens marched to the American legation to present a medal of gratitude.Woodrow Wilson Polish Relief Statement (ca. early 1918): Hand-annotated presidential manuscript detailing his direct personal outreach to the King of England, the President of France, and the Emperors of Russia, Germany, and Austria; laments his heartbreaking failure to secure a unified diplomatic framework to send humanitarian food and refugee aid to war-torn Poland. Theodore Roosevelt Prophetic Peace Letter (December 21, 1917): Written during World War I to a British officer; explicitly warns that forcing an "inconclusive peace" on Germany at this stage will inevitably result in an even "more destructive war in the future"—a warning validated two decades later by WWII. Theodore Roosevelt Cuban Treaty Instrument (November 10, 1903): Official typed White House state letter submitting the U.S.-Cuba treaty to the Senate for ratification; effectuated the highly controversial Platt Amendment, establishing the Guantánamo naval base and American intervention rights while explicitly recognizing Cuban independence. Theodore Roosevelt News Scheme Letter (July 22, 1903): A hand-annotated presidential note to the editor of Leslie’s Weekly magazine regarding a hope that published financial experts will coordinate an economic policy he can back. William Tecumseh Sherman Anti-Patronage Letter (November 6, 1874): A remarkably bitter 4-page personal letter written as Commander of the Army; fiercely lambastes his former Civil War comrade, President Ulysses S. Grant, for abandoning old battlefield friends to appease selfish Washington politicians, while recalling how Andrew Johnson had previously manipulated them both. John H. Surratt, Jr. War Department Letter (November 10, 1863): Signed twice by the notorious Confederate courier and Lincoln assassination conspirator; requests an appointment from the U.S. Assistant Secretary of War just six weeks before his fateful introduction to John Wilkes Booth. Zachary Taylor Political Defiance Letter (August 26, 1848): Written on the campaign trail less than a year before ascending to the presidency; fiercely rebuffs northern newspaper accounts regarding his stance on the Wilmot Proviso and expansion of slavery, while dismissing separate public charges of personal intemperance as "frivolous and absurd." Ulysses S. Grant Travel Despatch (August 8, 1868): Lined Army Headquarters letter written in pencil by General Grant to an Illinois contact, coordinating an early arrival.Ulysses S. Grant Clipped Autographs (1881/Undated): A pair of clipped signatures, one framed alongside a classic steel engraving of General Grant reading a map on a battlefield. Harry S. Truman Convention Letter (August 29, 1956): Post-presidential letter to Dean Acheson taking credit for aggressively reviving a "dead" 1956 Democratic National Convention; explicitly defends his controversial decision to endorse Averell Harriman over Adlai Stevenson and compares political losers to Al Smith's legacy of bitterness toward FDR. Harry S. Truman "Ass Kicker" Letter (April 20, 1955): A colorful personal note to Dean Acheson following a high-profile appearance before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; explicitly declares that he has no interest in acting like an elegant "elder statesman," stating he prefers being a "nose buster and an ass kicker." Harry S. Truman Eisenhower Criticism Letter (December 7, 1956): A blistering 2-page letter to Dean Acheson lambasting the Eisenhower White House for a "do nothing attitude" toward global Communism; heavily criticizes Eisenhower's handling of the Suez Crisis and the Soviet invasion of Hungary, calling his administration's foreign policy a "fake sanctimonious and counterfeit prayer approach." Harry S. Truman White House Balcony Art (ca. 1952): Humorous custom ink-and-watercolor presentation artwork commissioned by Truman as a wedding gift for key advisor George Elsey; depicts Truman and Averell Harriman standing on the president's highly controversial, newly constructed White House second-story balcony. Harry S. Truman Cabinet Portrait (August 25, 1950): Oversized boardroom photograph signed by Truman and his entire core cabinet; captured on the historic day the president ordered the U.S. Army to seize national railroads to avert a crippling workers' strike. Harry S. Truman "Truman Lighter" Gift (ca. 1949): A customized Ritepoint liquid table lighter inside its original box, featuring an embedded portrait of Truman at his desk; inscribed by the president as a personal gift to his historic 1948 "whistle-stop" campaign partner, Vice President Alben Barkley. Harry S. Truman Douglas MacArthur Letter (April 26, 1951): A critical presidential letter written to the manager of the Chicago Sun-Times just two weeks after relieving General Douglas MacArthur of his command in Korea; fiercely reasserts the foundational constitutional principle that "military commanders are subordinate to civil authority." Harry S. Truman Succession Precedent Letter (December 7, 1948): A White House letter to a young schoolgirl explaining Article II of the Constitution; utilizes John Tyler's historical succession following William Henry Harrison's death to prove that a Vice President becomes the true President in fact. Harry S. Truman Early Presidential Anxiety Letter (May 12, 1945): Written exactly one month to the day after assuming office following FDR's sudden death; confides to a friend that he had always been "fearful that responsibility would be mine" and laments that the presidency strips away his freedom to interact casually with everyday citizens. Harry S. Truman Congressional Support Letter (May 2, 1945): A prompt White House note thanking a representative for expressions of condolence and support following the tragic passing of Franklin D. Roosevelt. John Tyler Emergency Cabinet Assembly (1841): Historic handwritten executive order penned on black-bordered mourning stationery immediately following the death of William Henry Harrison; marks the exact moment Tyler assumed the full office of the presidency, shattering cabinet contentions that he was merely an "acting" executive and solidifying the American constitutional precedent of succession. Dwight D. Eisenhower Campaign Letter (July 23, 1952): Written from Denver to an Oregon publisher during the peak of his 1952 presidential run; includes an inner program leaf co-signed by both Dwight and Mamie Eisenhower. Jimmy Doolittle Signed Declaration of War (December 8, 1941): A typed transcript of the official U.S. Declaration of War against the Imperial Government of Japan following Pearl Harbor, signed by the legendary aviation general. Amelia Earhart Newark-Chicago Aviation Card (September 8, 1930): Red pencil signature across an official cardstock souvenir commemorating the First Direct Flight between Newark and Chicago. Amelia Earhart Boston Dinner Program (June 29, 1932): National Aeronautic Association dinner program signed by Earhart just weeks after her historic solo transatlantic flight, featuring a custom commemorative poem titled "Pioneers." Thomas Jefferson Revenue Appointment Letter (March 4, 1791): Sent as the first U.S. Secretary of State; officially transmits President Washington's appointment of a Revenue Supervisor for Rhode Island. This document was executed just one day after the passage of the highly controversial Excise Act, which divided the nation into 14 revenue collection districts and ultimately triggered the armed uprising known as the Whiskey Rebellion. Thomas Jefferson Clipped Signature (Undated): A bold, handwritten autograph clipped from an official vellum document. Abraham Lincoln Military Appointment (April 26, 1862): A vellum commission co-signed by Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton; officially names an Assistant Quartermaster of Volunteers during the early, transformative operational phases of the Civil War. Abraham Lincoln Paymaster Appointment (July 2, 1862): A presidential vellum document co-signed by Edwin M. Stanton; formally commissions an Additional Paymaster to oversee Union troop financing. Abraham Lincoln Executive Mansion Note (July 23, 1864): A brief, wartime presidential command written on official letterhead; instructs a bearer to retrieve and deliver the official military papers regarding a specific captain's case. Andrew Johnson Carte de Visite (Undated): A formal presidential portrait photograph tipped onto a card signed along the lower margin. Carl Linnaeus Academic Letter (April 4, 1750): Written in Old Swedish during his tenure as Rector of Uppsala University to the university's secretary. This historic academic correspondence was executed the exact same year Linnaeus published Philosophia Botanica and just three years prior to his seminal Species Plantarum, which permanently established the modern binomial nomenclature framework for plant taxonomy. Theodor Herzl Literary Correspondence (October 24, 1890): Written from Germany to a close confidant regarding the scheduled rehearsals of his play Die Dame in Schwarz at Vienna's prestigious Burgtheater. This letter captures Herzl's early life as a European playwright and journalist, years before his assignment to cover the explosive Dreyfus Affair prompted him to write The Jewish State and establish the World Zionist Organization. Alexander Graham Bell Houseboat Letter (April 17, 1917): A lengthy, deeply personal 4-page letter written from his Nova Scotia estate to his wife Mabel in Washington, D.C.. Bell details a grueling, icy, multi-day wilderness journey home that was successfully navigated entirely by coordinating rescue efforts over the telephone. This artifact is extraordinarily rare as it represents the only known correspondence where the legendary inventor explicitly references his own practical use of the telephone. Yuri Gagarin Moon Program Manuscript (January 24, 1968): A carbon-typewritten scientific research paper in Russian featuring extensive corrections and a hand-drawn array of aerodynamic diagrams on the reverse of each leaf. Prepared during his studies at the Zhukowski Military Academy, this paper utilizes computer-aided numerical analysis and wind tunnel research to help advance the Soviet lunar landing program. It serves as a profoundly tragic artifact, as its complex mathematical calculations regarding an aircraft's flight angle of attack directly foreshadowed the flight-training crash that claimed Gagarin's life just two months later. Dalai Lama Tibetan Youth Message (May 25, 1989): A typed English message featuring a full signature penned in Tibetan script, sent from his exile in Dharamsala, India. The spiritual leader imparts moral guidance to the next generation, emphasizing that true education requires the internal development of honesty, compassion, and resilience. The document carries immense historical weight, as it was written less than five months before the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded him the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize. Ayn Rand Anti-Communist Resistance Letter (October 14, 1937): Written on separate sheets from New York to a prominent executive assistant at Selznick International Pictures in Hollywood. Rand passionately vents her frustration and indignation over Broadway producers dropping her theatrical adaptation of We the Living. She explicitly charges that a "Red friends" network had established a powerful "unofficial censorship of their own" across American theater, heavily suppressing any works carrying a explicitly anti-Soviet or individual-versus-the-state theme. Winston Churchill Post-War Aviation Draft (June 1943): A heavily annotated, unsigned draft page from his official "Post-War Civil Aviation" report, which is cross-referenced with British War Cabinet papers. Reworked entirely in Churchill's red ink, the prime minister actively rejects a fully internationalized, "cosmopolitan" global airline model. He strategically details a plan to entangle American commercial interests within a loosely regulated universal framework, aiming to transform rising U.S. aviation power from a major external threat into a primary bulwark for the post-war British Empire. John F. Kennedy Inscribed Tokens Photograph (Undated): An oversized gelatin silver portrait signed by the President and inscribed to musician Joe Venneri, a member of the chart-topping musical group The Tokens. John F. Kennedy Seated Portrait (Undated): A signed photograph depicting a youthful Jack Kennedy seated at a table alongside two associates, inscribed "with warm regards a decade later". Lyndon B. Johnson & Jackie Kennedy Urban Rejuvenation Archive (1968–1972): An exchange of historical correspondence addressed to Daniel Patrick Moynihan regarding the grand architectural rehabilitation of Pennsylvania Avenue. Includes a December 1968 letter from President Johnson on White House stationery passing the legislative torch to the next administration, alongside deeply moving personal letters from Jacqueline Kennedy written from Athens and New York, fiercely thanking Moynihan for his lifelong devotion to preserving JFK's structural and aesthetic vision for the nation's capital. Douglas MacArthur United Nations Flag Quotation (July 14, 1950): A handwritten, signed historic quotation inscribed onto an official battlefield photograph. Captured in Tokyo on the exact day U.S. Army Chief of Staff J. Lawton Collins presented him with the U.N. flag, MacArthur proudly proclaims his command's commitment to "uphold this noble ideal," hailing the banner as a global symbol of man's struggle to free himself. This marks his historic appointment by President Truman as the very first supreme commander of a multi-national coalition combatting open international aggression. Charles Lindbergh Englewood Broadway Letter (November 27, 1932): Penned on his custom New York business letterhead; coordinates the personal signing of historic airmail covers. Charles Lindbergh Export Sworn Declaration (September 20, 1929): The signed lower half of an official U.S. Customs export document certifying that no live livestock would be exported on his flight. Charles Lindbergh First Flight Commemorative Cover (April 15, 1926): An official, legal-sized airmail envelope co-signed by Lindbergh as pilot and the local postmaster to celebrate his historic, early Chicago-to-St. Louis mail route. Charles Lindbergh Pan-American Flight Declaration (October 20, 1929): An official Port of New York customs document signed immediately following a flight from Paramaribo, Suriname; certifies that he, his wife, and his co-pilot successfully landed in Miami with no dutiable personal household effects. Ronald Reagan Gallery Project Letter (March 16, No Year): A polite, handwritten letter to an individual explaining that the Reagan family has only recently begun collecting a modest array of artwork to decorate their bare home walls. Ronald Reagan Publicity Portraits (Undated): A collection of four separate gelatin silver publicity photographs spanning his career from a young Hollywood actor to a middle-aged public figure, each uniquely inscribed to various recipients. The Gilded Age Literary Scrapbook Leaves (1902–1922): A collection of vintage scrapbook pages containing a grouping of clipped signatures from prominent American writers, including Samuel Clemens ("Mark Twain"), Edward Everett Hale, Kate Douglas Wiggin, and W.D. Howells. The Multi-Generational Political Autograph Lot (1898–1969): A broad signature lot spanning multiple decades of American history. Features an April 1898 Spanish-American War-era Navy Department letter signed by Assistant Secretary Theodore Roosevelt; a 1967 Republican Association program signed by California Governor Ronald Reagan; a 1961 personal letter from five-star General Douglas MacArthur; a four-star General letter from Omar N. Bradley; and a custom note from "Believe It Or Not" illustrator Robert Ripley. Harry S. Truman Victory & Portrait Archive (1965–1968): A grouping of three post-presidential signatures, highlighted by an August 1968 hand-signed copy of his iconic, smiling photograph triumphantly holding up the infamously incorrect Chicago Daily Tribune "Dewey Defeats Truman" election headline. George Washington Presidential Ship's Protection (December 10, 1794): Executed from Alexandria, Virginia; a large, official maritime passport printed in parallel columns of French, English, and Dutch. Bearing the original crisp white wafer seal of the presidency, this protective state document grants safe passage to the brig The Peggy to transport a vital cargo of American flour, wheat, and corn to the Atlantic island of Madeira. It carries massive structural significance as a fully executed piece of early Federalist federal diplomacy, co-signed by early American legends including Collector of Customs John Fitzgerald, Alexandria Mayor Robert Mease, and U.S. Secretary of State Edmund Randolph. Vincent van Gogh Final Year Letter (1890): A handwritten letter in French penned during the final, tumultuous months of his life. Van Gogh shares a poignant philosophical observation on the fragile nature of human existence, writing that "illnesses are there to make us remember again that we are not made of wood". Thomas Jefferson Address to the Cherokee Nation (1806): An extraordinary, museum-grade handwritten manuscript signed by Jefferson during his first term as President. This historic executive document contains the full, formal diplomatic address he personally delivered to the assembled Chiefs of the Cherokee Nation, outlining the early federal government's official policies regarding native territories, borders, and co-existence. selected.title: ANYWHERE - 2 - a mediterranean trip
selected.description: And so, as it goes, at this point, I may be somewhere on the border area between south Portugal and south Spain, slowly walking on the side of some kind of motorway going across a swamp sort of thing, now, watching the wader birds hopping through the ponds around, this is, probably migratory creatures coming from the other side of the strait, I mean, from Africa, and then, as I think about the p ossible trajectories these birds would do in order to get here, how they manage to n escape the Sahara winds etc, at some point, I would get a ride in a transporter, say, that kind of vans transporting furniture and home stuff from old addresses to new addresses. And well, as soon as I get in, Yan, the driver’s name, a middle aged guy with blond hair, goatee and sideburns, immediately says that he’s actually on the way to Gibraltar, plus, “after a small stop in Sevilla, I should be on the way to the south again” he adds, and, “oh, that suits me perfectly... that’s exactly where I wanna go!” I say, “Gibraltar?”, “yes, Gibraltar, Algeciras, and then Barcelona, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, and then north Africa, I mean, I wanna go all around the Mediterranean sea, and come back to Spain through Morocco!!”, “Oh,” he says, and then, “that seems tough!” he adds while showing some kind of intrigued smile, hence, thereupon, after we have actually passed Ayamonte, the first town in Spain, “actually I was born in the Balkans...” he says, “my mother was from there, just my father is English… this meaning that, well, I spent part of my childhood in different islands of the Aegean Sea… places like Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Naxos, and so on… and well, I also may say that… at some point, my best friends there, in this islands, were mainly the sons and the daughters of the A-zian refugees living on the campsites nearby…. and then, on my teens, well, I was sent to an auntie in Italy, and then, to another relative in France, and just then, I went to visit the old family in North Yorkshire, where I spent four or five year doing some schooling… that, before getting into a parade with a bunch of con hippies that would drive me away from Europe into Anatolian lands, I mean east Turkey, and then Iran, Afghanistan, Nepal, Laos, Vietnam… the Siam area, I mean Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore, and just then, from Indonesia into Australia we went… I mean, we would pass through many Indonesian islands, places like Java, Bali, Lombok, West Nusa Tenggara, East Nusa Tenggara, Timor and other smaller ones…'', he says, and “Uoou, whata big journey!” I would exclaim, and then, “What about Australia, how was it?” I ask, and he, “pretty boring... I mean, soon I would pass myself into New Zealand where people are more... yeah, once there, soon I would jump onto a big ship that would take me across the pacific ocean, South America, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil, and then… the Caribbeans…”; “Ohu, looks amazing, I myself I have only been in Mexico… what about you, in which islands of Caribbeans have you been?” I would ask. And once there, instantly, I get inside some blue Ship that takes me across the Helenic sea to the Chios island, the home town of Mastika, a liqueur seasoned with mastic, a resin with a slightly pine or cedar-like flavour. And so, from Chios I take another small ferry into Turkey mainland, more precisely to Chesme, a word that means “fountain” in the T u rk ish language, and, from Chesme I pass to Izmir, or Smyrna , a city that was completely burned at the beginning of the twentieth century. Thus, I disembark in konak, I pass the Kemeraltı Çarşısı, a huge street market, and I go up the Kadifekale Dağı, or the Kadifekale hill, a shanty town, before inhabited by Greeks and Armenians, now a hub for gypsies, Syrian refugees and Mevlevis. And so, I go up the Mount Pagos (being Pagos a derivation from the word pagus , that is the origin of the word meaning “country” in Romance languages, and the root of other words like pays (French), país (Spanish), and more remotely, for the English word "peasant" and the corresponding adjective paganus that became the term "pagan") and so, as I arrive to the top of the hill where is the ruins of the Kadifekale, or Kadife castle, I move inside its fortress inhabited by some female pine trees and there in the middle of this small groove, I find this small stall with a guy serving teas. And so, it is here inside the ruined fortress that I meet Reza, an Iranian guy from Tehran, and Anneli, a girl from Finland, being Anneli “grace” a contraction of the name Annalise, which itself is a combination of Anna and Liese. And so, after getting to know this, I go down the Pagos mount with them, and as we go down, we visit the ruins of the Agora , a word that means “assembly" in ancient Greek language. This is, historically, the Agora was the centre of the athletic, artistic, business, social, spiritual, and political life in any ancient Greek city. And then, after leaving this city, I’m already hitchhiking south, and so, I pass Aydın, that means illuminated, I pass Bodrum and Marmaris, a city in front of the Greek island of Rhodes, an island that inspired a song from Portishead. And it is here, that I get a ride with an economics student, and as it goes, we talk about the difference between the Turkish lira and the american dollar, and then I get a ride with a van carrying packages of crisps, this man would take me Fethiye, and then some kind of touristic van takes me to Antalya and Alanya, and well, once on the border, some Kurdish soldiers even help me to cross into Syria , and so, as I go through Syria all gets dark, and then, when I wake up, I’m already floating over the dead sea. Further, after crossing the Sinai desert, I end up in Port Said, in north Egypt, a city established about one half hundred years ago, during the building of the Suez Canal. This is, in this city, there are numerous old houses with grand balconies on all floors, giving the city an impression of holidays-in colony, but that isn't the case. And so, during some days I explore the port area, I wander around the loading and unloading areas, watching the huge container ships arriving from China, Japan, India, some countries in Africa, etc. And as it goes, someone tells me that there are about one hundred of them arriving here every day, from both sides, including tanker ships, bulk ships, container ships and general cargo ships, being China, the most frequent customer. And so, I end up making friends on the port, plus, they even offer me work there. So, after less than one week here, helping to load and unload the ships on the port, arranging the loads in the warehouses and also, serving as translator from time to time, coz actually, I can speak some Arab, English and a bunch of Latin languages. Thus, with the time, I would get to know that this city was actually founded by many foreigners during the construction of the Suez channel. And since its foundation people of many nationalities and religions had been moving to this city and each community brought in its own customs, cuisine, religion, architecture, etc. As time went by, the old Arab Quarter was actually swallowed up into a thriving city, and the bustling international community included, between others, Jewish merchants, Italian architects, Swiss hoteliers, Maltese administrators, Scottish engineers, French bankers, Greek opportunity hunters, and diplomats from all around the world. But nowadays, things are a bit different, everything is much more mixed, there is no more big difference between Arabs and Europeans, and “there are also some Africans working here, mainly people from Sudan or Eritrea”, they say. Thus, on the going, I would make friendship with a couple of guys from Bangladesh too, they said they used to work in Dubai, years ago, when there was a boom of construction in the Emirates United, and so, in the meanwhile, they would came here, temporarily, as a way of transferring themselves to Europe, but, there was some problems with their documents and they ended up staying here. Thus, after some weeks on the port working with those people, at some point, I would board a ship full of cotton and nitrogenous fertilizers with Tripoli as destination, this is, Libya, the neighbor country, that is trying to recover from a series of failed revolutions after Qaddafi’s disappearance. And so, already on the going, cruising the Mediterranean, as we enter in Libya waters, our conversation goes exactly around Qaddafi sons and daughters, and someone from the ship crew say Qaddafi have ten sons and ten daughters, and some others say he was an impotent man, and others say he may have more than one hundred sons and daughters spread through Africa, Europe and the Arab world. And so, now they talk about Muhammad Muammar Qaddafi, his elder son, regarded as a possible successor of his father, but reported to be uninterested in the role. “Some years ago he was involved in an armed standoff with his half-brother Mutassim over control of a Coca-Cola bottling plant" says one of the men aboard. “And one of his children was killed by a NATO airstrike along with his half-brother Saif al-Arab Qaddafi” another one says. “Later, he surrendered to rebel forces of the National Transitional Council as they took over Tripoli... and some say he’s now in Oman, since they granted him political asylum over there, a long time ago”. “And after there is Saif al-Islam...  the second of Qaddafi´s son, from a different mother… an arrest warrant was issued by the International Criminal Court for charges of crimes against humanity against the Libyan people, for killing and persecuting civilians, but he denied all this… and  after the end of the Civil War, he flown by plane and was sentenced to death by a court in Tripoli for crimes during the civil war, in a widely criticized trial conducted in absentia … later his full amnesty was declared and he even attempted to register as a candidate in a recent presidential election, but was rejected and once again disappeared…”. “Then we have Al-Saadi, the football star, he played for the Italian teams Perugia, Udinese and Sampdoria, playing only some minutes in a couple of matches, and employing Diego Maradona as his technical consultant… he would become the leader of Libya's Special Forces… and later arrested in Niger, people say, he's now residing in Turkey…”. “Then we have, Mutassim Billah Gaddafi, assassinated in the same year as his father, he was a Libyan Army officer, and the National Security Advisor of Libya… he even met the U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, asking her some billions, to form his own special forces brigade, with material from Russia, China, and the United States… he lived in Egypt for several years after allegedly attempting to take control of Libya from his father… he would often travel to Roma, London and Paris, in his private jet, and would frequent the plus expansive hairdressers… where he would play his seduction games, and one of his famous girlfriends was a model named Talitha Van something…”. “Then there is Hannibal Gaddafi, who graduated from the Marine Academy of Maritime Studies… and later married a Lebanese Christian former lingerie model, with whom he has three children… he was arrested in Geneva, Switzerland, after an incident in his hotel… and later was involved in another turmoil in another hotel, this time in London… he, his wife, and a local woman, were found in the room bleeding heavily… then, during the revolution times, after the rebels entered Tripoli, Qaddafi and his wife fled to Algeria together with other members of the Qaddafi… and later he would move to Syria with his wife and children… and later, an Ethiopian nanny who cared for the couple's young daughter and son was found abandoned by the rebels in a room at one of the family's luxury seaside villas in western Tripoli. She claimed that they tied her up, taped her mouth and while one would pour boiling water on her head, the other would slashed her with knives… later, after the revolution, Hannibal was kidnapped and briefly held in Lebanon by an armed group demanding information about the disappearance of a certain Shiite Imam… but later was released and an arrest warrant was issued against him by the Lebanese government… a request by the Syrian government to return Qaddafi on the grounds that he was a political refugee was denied by the Lebanese government… and later Russian officials would offer him asylum in Moscow… and then we have Saif al-Arab Gaddafi, the sixth son of the Gaddafi despot, this one used to live in Munich… and so, excessive noise from the exhaust of his Ferrari led to questions from the German police and his car being impounded… Also, during the same period, Saif was suspected of attempting to smuggle an assault rifle, a revolver and munitions from Munich to Paris in a car with diplomatic number plates… However, the case was later dropped as the alleged weapons were never found and the German public prosecutor decided that there was insufficient evidence to proceed with a prosecution… following the outbreak of the Libyan Civil War, the German press reported that Saif al-Arab had returned to Libya. Subsequently, the Bavarian Interior Ministry stated that he had been declared persona non-grata and in the aftermath of that, United Nations Security Council imposed a travel ban on Saif al-Arab and an Interpol notice was then issued against him… an air strike on Saif al-Arab's house had killed Saif al-Arab, along with three of Muammar Qaddafi’s   grandchildren… and then Khamis Qaddafi, the seventh and youngest son of the former leader, was the military commander in charge of the Khamis Brigade of the Libyan Army… At age three, Khamis Qaddafi was injured in the US. bombing of Libya, suffering head injuries when the Bab al-Azizia military compound was attacked in retaliation for the Berlin discotheque bombing… plus, he graduated from the military academy in Tripoli, receiving a bachelor's degree in military arts and science, further graduating from the Frunze Military Academy in Moscow and the Military Academy of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Russia… Khamis, who was said to be uninterested in politics, rose in prominence due to the exile of his older brother Mutassim, who was sent to Egypt in 2001 after being accused by senior officials of plotting to seize power from his father… Muammar Qaddafi ordered the disbandment of Mutassim's Tank Battalion and created the Reinforced Brigade known as Khamis Brigade in its place… By most accounts, Khamis was competent, loyal to his father, and maintained good relationships with his siblings… He was especially close to his reformist older brother Saif al-Islam and began a master's degree at the IE Business School in Madrid. However, he was expelled by the institution for his links to the attacks against the Libyan population… so, after hurrying back to Libya to aid his father in the civil war, Khamis commanded the assault on Zawiya, leading the Khamis Brigade… and the battle resulted in pro-Gaddafi forces retaking the city… but later was reported by the anti-Gaddafi Al Manara Media that Khamis had died from injuries of an a ir plane that supposedly crashed against him… a NATO aeroplane… and then there is Ayesha Qaddafi, the only biological daughter with his second wife Safia Farkash. Ayesha was educated at the Paris Diderot University, and studied law at the Sorbonne. She trained with the Libyan military, reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel. In 2000 after sanctions were imposed on Iraq, she arrived in Baghdad with a delegation of 69 officials, and shortly before the invasion of Iraq, she met with Saddam Hussein… later she would sued NATO over the bombing of a building in her father's compound which she alleged killed her brother, Saif al-Arab Qaddafi, and her own infant daughter. Later, during the revolution, along with two of her brothers and other family members, she left Algeria to go to Oman, where other members of the Q addaf i family are currently living…”. And so, now, as we get out in the port of Algiers, I cross the Rampe Magenta and enter a piazza garden with some small palm trees and a bandstand in the middle, a nouvelle vague bandstand like the ones I have seen in some gardens in Lisbon. And they tell me this is the Port Saïd Square. Then I go along the Abane Ramdane street, there is a huge building on my right with a series of arches and on my left I see a store named Miss Dunya Lissa, a clothes shop with some old fashioned pajamas for women, slightly risky necklines, lacy sleeves, like the female nightwear of the 80s, then a couple of shops with home goods like towels, bedspreads, aprons, trench coats, toilet brushes, etc, then I pass the Hotel Akfado, a couple of boutiques more, raw perfumes stores, the Motel Odeon capsules, the Redouan Episse, that is selling packaged spices and some different kinds of roots, and I arrive at an archaeological excavation site, named Quartier Ottoman de la Basse Casbah. I keep going through the lane Bab El Oued, I pass some carpet stores and I arrive at the Martyrs' Square, a square with some more palm trees and a couple of minarets in the back. Then I turn left and I go up through a series of narrow staircases, and at some point, I arrive at the Palais Dar Ahmed Pasha, this is, from here I can see the coast and the sea, and the Dar Mustapha Pacha and the Dar Souf Palace. Then I go through the Rue de l'Indépendance and I arrive at the Rue du Diable, which is a staircase inside a tunnel, and on the top of it there is an old man, seated on the balustrade, he greets me, I greet him and we act out a conversation. I ask him why this alley is named “devil street” and he tells me about Barbarossa, the famous pirate of the “albahr al'abyad almutawasit”, the mediterranean sea. He tells me that he used to come here into these alleys, looking for girls. “Originally named Khayr al-Din Barbarus , also known as Hayreddin Pasha, romanticized Barbarossa by the Italians...” he tells me in french language, . “was an Ottoman corsair and later admiral of the Ottoman Navy, by Suleiman the Magnificent, that great pasha famous for the Siege of Vienna.… Barbarossa was actually born in Lesbos, the Greek/Turkish island on the aegean sea, and began his naval career as a corsair under his elder brother Oruç Reis, that captured Algiers from Spain, then following Oruç's death, Khayr inherited his brother's achievements and became one of the most feared man in the Mediterranean… he captures Tunis, Gibraltar, Sicil y and some other Greek islands…” and then, after saying this things, the old man stands up and makes me signal to accompany him, and so, he takes me precisely to the Barbarous street, which is just some alleys up, and from there we enter another alley named Rue Kataroudjil and in some minutes we debouch at a kind of natural balcony, from where we can see all the Bay of Algiers. Next morning I come back to the port and I manage to board another small ship that goes in the direction of the Morocco coast. Apparently the ship is carrying a cargo of detergents, things made in China, that were exported to Libya, but Libya discarded them to Tunisia, and Tunisia discarded it to Algeria, and now, Algeria is passing it to Morocco. And so, as we go along the M oroccan coast, we pass cities like Saidia, Nador,  Al Hoceima, El Jebha, and then, Tétouan and Tangier, where I disembark, and then, there I go, in the direction of Cape Spartel, where is the Spartel Bank, a sunken island hypothesized by some as being the location of the legendary Atlantis islan d.

selected.description: وصف برناند لويس من اعتنقوا الإسلام خلال الفترة الحديثة 1500-1800م "بالمغامرين؛ ولا يعدو أن يكونوا قلّة"؛ لكن يبدو أن الواقع يتجاوز مجرد "المغامرة”، فأمام تزايد عدد المعتنقين للإسلام حذّر الكتاب ومنظمات الفدية القراء بإخبارهم "أنّ أغلب الذين أخذوا أسرى من قبل "المغاربة"؛ تخلّو عن المذهب أو الإيمان ‘ Faith’ " ، في حين هاجر آخرون إلى البلاد المغاربية لاعتناقه طوعا. وليس هذا فقط، بل صّرح دي سوسا في عمله أنّ نصف سكان الجزائر بين عامي 1580 و 1581 'كانوا من المهتدين'. وأما روبيرت بيرتن فبعد قراءته عن الأعداد الهائلة التي اعتنقت الإسلام بتونس والجزائر، فقد استنتج أن "المسيحيين الذين اعتنقوا الإسلام... رحب بهم كإخوة"، وبشيء من السخرية أكد ساموال هارتليب في "عريضته" سنة 1644 أن الفقر دفع العديد ممن يرغبون في عيش حياة شريفة إلى الاحتيال، الكذب، السرقة، القتل، واعتناق الإسلام   Turn Turk أو أي شيء آخر". hhhgg وفي مسرحية سيرفانتس 1580 " El Trato de Argel "   هتف الأسير أورليو بأن الإسلام قد اجتاح المسيحيين كبارا وصغاراً". إن الإسلام خلال القرن السابع عشر كان ذا قوة جاذبة، جعلت الآلاف من النصارى يتخلون عن دينهم. ولهذا فقد دعم السياسيون والكنسيّون الأدبيات التي تسيء للإسلام والمسلمين. فقد كتب هوكلايت: "أن الجزائر هي عرش القرصنة ومفسدة التجارة، ومركز العبودية... ووكر شياطين البحر، وعاء المرتدين وخونة بلدانهم"، في حين نشرت إحدى الجرائد البريطانية سنة 1609م : "المسيحيون جعلوا مسلمين والمسلمون أبناء الشيطان" أما شكسبير في مسرحيته العاصفة "فقد وصف الجزائر بموطن الساحرات والخارجين عن القانون ".

selected.title: Don Quijote
selected.description: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (Alcalá de Henares,​ 29 de septiembre de 1547-Madrid, 22 de abril​ de 1616) fue un novelista, poeta, dramaturgo y soldado español. Es ampliamente considerado una de las máximas figuras de la literatura española. Fue el autor de El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha, novela conocida habitualmente como El Quijote, que lo llevó a ser mundialmente conocido y a la cual muchos críticos han descrito como la primera novela moderna, así como una de las mejores obras de la literatura universal, cuya cantidad de ediciones y traducciones solo es superada por la Biblia.​ A Cervantes se le ha dado el apelativo de «Príncipe de los Ingenios» Infancia y juventud Torre de la iglesia de Santa María la Mayor de Alcalá de Henares, donde bautizaron a Miguel de Cervantes. Resultó destruida en un incendio durante la guerra civil española.Desde el siglo XVIII está admitido que el lugar de nacimiento de Miguel de Cervantes fue Alcalá de Henares,4​ dado que allí fue bautizado, según su acta bautismal, y que de allí aclaró ser natural en la llamada Información de Argel (1580).

selected.title: ERIC ED046274: Cautivos Precervantinos, Cara y Cruz del Cautiverio (Pre-Cervantine Captives and the Condition of Their Captivity).
selected.description: Miguel de Cervantes' capture by the Turks and his imprisonment in Argel (Morocco) during the Battle of Lepanto in the sixteenth century have been studied by literary critics who have endeavored to determine fiction and reality in certain episodes of "Don Quijote" and in the drama, "Los banos de Argel". Twelve documents published here provide background data on Spanish prisoners held captive in Tetuan, Argel, and Velez. From the testimony presented and the similarities suggested, it is apparent that Cervantes drew his inspiration from real life experience. The linguistic, lexical, and idiomatic aspects of the documents are scrutinized to understand Cervantes' aesthetics. An abundance of information is offered on the prisoners including their dress, manners, speech, manner of capture, and the desolation, anguish and misery experienced. In addition to the actual documents, the appendix also includes a glossary of key words appearing in the texts. (DS)

On August 3, 1948, Time magazine editor Whittaker Chambers made a stunning allegation before the House Un-American Activities Committee: Alger Hiss, president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and former high-ranking State Department official, had served with him in the Communist underground. From Wikipedia; The American Magazine  was a  periodical publication  founded in June 1906, a continuation of failed publications purchased a few years earlier from publishing mogul  Miriam Leslie . It succeeded  Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly  (1876–1904),  Leslie's Monthly Magazine  (1904–1905),  Leslie's Magazine  (1905) and the  American Illustrated Magazine  (1905–1906). [ 1 ]  The magazine was published through August 1956. History [ edit ] Under the magazine's original title,  Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly , it had begun to be published in 1876 and was renamed  Leslie's Monthly Magazine  in 1904, and then was renamed again as  Leslie's Magazine  in 1905. [ 2 ]  From September 1905, through May 1906, it was entitled the  American Illustrated Magazine ; then subsequently shortened as  The American Magazine  until publication ceased in 1956. It kept continuous volume numbering throughout its history. [ 2 ] In June 1906,  muckraking   journalists   Ray Stannard Baker ,  Lincoln Steffens  and  Ida M. Tarbell  left  McClure's  to help create  The American Magazine . An "Editorial Announcement" published in 1907 led with Tarbell's coverage of tariff policy. [ 3 ]  Baker contributed articles using the pseudonym  David Grayson . Under  John Sanborn Phillips , who served as editor until 1915, the monthly magazine departed somewhat from the muckraking style and focused on human interest stories, social issues and fiction. Initially published by his Phillips Publishing Company of  Springfield ,  Ohio , it later was taken over by Crowell Publishing Company in 1911, [ 4 ]  and later merged with  Collier's .  The American Magazine  was published by  Crowell-Collier  until it folded in 1956. [ 5 ] Editors [ edit ] With the changes in 1915, John M. Siddall (1915–23) was appointed as editor of the periodical, which expanded its market considerably by concentrating on a female readership. The cover of the September 1917 issue announced: "This Magazine's Circulation Has Doubled in 20 Months." The September 1922 cover stated circulation had reached 1.8 million. Merle Crowell served as editor of  The American Magazine  from 1923 until 1929 when  Sumner Blossom  took over. Blossom, who had been editor of  Popular Science , was there for the last 27 years of the magazine's existence. Fictional  serials  and  short stories  were a popular feature, and the magazine published several winners of the  O. Henry Awards . High-profile writers contributed articles on a variety of topics. During his editorship, Blossom adopted the policy of hiding the author's name on all works of fiction during the selection process as a way to encourage new fiction writers. The magazine's staff learned the author's identity only once they accepted or rejected a manuscript. The last issue of  The American Magazine  was displayed on newsstands in August 1956. [ 6 ] Stories [ edit ] In 1934,  The American Magazine  ran a story called "Uncle Sam Grows Younger" that praised  Alger Hiss : "In his twenties, he is one of the men chiefly responsible for the plan to buy $650,000,000 worth of commodities to feed the unemployed. He has too much spirit for his bodily strength and is in danger of working himself to death." [ 7 ] Notable contributors [ edit ] Bess Streeter Aldrich Sherwood Anderson Harry J. Anslinger J. selected.title: A torch kept lit : great lives of the twentieth century
description: 323 pages : 22 cm

"A unique collection of eulogies of the twentieth century's greatest figures, written by conservative icon William F. Buckley Jr. and compiled by National Review and Fox News chief Washington correspondent James Rosen. In a half-century on the national stage, William F. Buckley Jr. achieved unique stature as a polemicist and the undisputed godfather of modern American conservatism. He knew everybody, hosted everybody at his East 73rd Street maisonette, skewered everybody who needed skewering, and in general lived life on a scale, and in a swashbuckling manner, that captivated and inspired countless young conservatives across that half-century. Among all of his distinctions, which include founding the conservative magazine National Review and serving as host on the long running talk show Firing Line, Buckley was a master of that most elusive of art forms: the eulogy. Buckley drew on his unrivaled gifts in what he liked to call 'the controversial arts' to mourn, celebrate, or seek eternal mercy for the men and women who touched his life and the nation; to conjure their personalities, recall memorable moments, herald their greatness; or to remind readers of why a given individual, even with the grace that death can uniquely confer, should be remembered as evil. At all points, these remembrances reflect Buckley's singular voice, with its elegant touch and mordant humor, and lend to the lives of the departed a final tribute consistent with their own careers, lives, and accomplishments. Of the more than 200 eulogies located in Buckley's vast archive of published works, A Torch Kept Lit collects the very best, those remembering the most consequential lives (Kennedy, Nixon, Reagan), the most famous to today's readers (Elvis Presley, John Lennon, Jacqueline Onassis, Princess Diana), those who loomed largest in the conservative movement (Milton Friedman, Russell Kirk), the most accomplished in the literary world (Norman Mailer, Truman Capote, William Shawn), the most mysterious (Soviet spy Alger Hiss, CIA spymaster Richard Helms), and those most dear to WFB (his wife and parents)"--
